results.title: Auto Tariffs 101: How U.S. Car Import Duties Really Work in 2025
results.content:
Engines, transmissions, electronic control units (ECUs), brakes, steering systems, and hundreds more
 Each imported part is taxed individually unless exempted (e.g., USMCA-compliant)
 As of May 3, 2025, a 25% rate applies to non-exempt parts

### 🔩 Materials (Steel, Aluminum)

 Tariffs on raw materials are handled separately — often 25–50%
 Automotive-specific tariffs usually override metal tariffs to prevent double taxation (“destacking” rules) [...] Most USMCA-compliant auto parts face 0% tariff under current rules. This applies to:

 Engines, electrical modules, and mechanical components
 Assemblies sourced or built in North America
 Aftermarket parts if manufactured in-region

However, manufacturers must retain and present thorough records proving origin — otherwise, the full 25% rate applies.

### 📌 Summary [...] If a component already faced a steel or aluminum tariff, it generally won’t be double-taxed under auto tariffs — the highest applicable rate applies.
 Classic cars (25+ years old) and some aftermarket parts may be exempt under separate categories.

results.title: FAQ: Import Duty & Taxes (Tariffs) on Car Parts Shipped from the UK to the USA | Flying Spares
results.content:
The type of car part (engine component, brake part, trim, electrical item, etc.)
 The material (metal, rubber, plastic, etc.)
 The declared value of the shipment
 The country of origin Most automotive parts fall under U.S. HTS (Harmonized Tariff Schedule) classifications in Chapter 87, but the duty rate can vary.

Your shipping carrier (e.g., DHL, FedEx, UPS) will usually contact you before delivery with the amount due.

Who is responsible for paying import duty (Tariffs) and fees? [...] In most cases, yes. When you order parts from Flying Spares in the UK and have them shipped to the United States, your order is considered an international import. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) may apply:

 Import duty (Tariffs) (based on the product classification)
 Customs processing fees
 State sales/use tax (in some cases)s
 Brokerage or clearance fees (charged by the carrier) [...] Seizure of goods
 Fines or penalties
 Delays in customs clearance

Are classic or vintage car parts treated differently?

No. Even if the parts are for classic or vintage vehicles (e.g., Rolls-Royce or Bentley models), they are still classified as automotive parts under U.S. customs regulations. The age of the vehicle typically does not eliminate import duty on replacement parts.
